questions.prompt: You receive an email from 'support@paypa1-security.com' saying your account is suspended and you must log in immediately via a link. What should you do?

options.text: Click the link and log in to fix the issue quickly
Ignore the email and go directly to the official PayPal website by typing the URL yourself
Reply to the email asking if it's real
Forward it to friends to warn them

questions.explanation: The domain 'paypa1-security.com' is a typosquat (digit '1' instead of letter 'l') and not PayPal's real domain. Never click links in urgent unsolicited emails — go directly to the official site instead.

questions.prompt: Which of these passwords is generally considered strongest?

options.text: P@ssw0rd1
MyDog2020!
correct-horse-battery-staple-42

questions.explanation: Length and unpredictability matter more than simple character substitution. A long random passphrase is harder to crack than short 'complex-looking' passwords that follow common patterns attackers already expect.

questions.prompt: What is the safest way to use important accounts (banking, email) while connected to public Wi-Fi?

options.text: Use them normally, public Wi-Fi is safe if the network has a password
Avoid sensitive logins on public Wi-Fi, or use a trusted VPN
Only use HTTP sites since HTTPS is slower
Turn off your antivirus to speed up the connection

questions.explanation: Public Wi-Fi can be monitored by attackers on the same network. Avoid sensitive activity on public Wi-Fi, or use a reputable VPN to encrypt your traffic.

questions.prompt: A colleague calls claiming to be from IT support and asks for your login password to 'fix an urgent issue.' What should you do?

options.text: Give the password since they claim to be from IT
Refuse, and verify the request through an official IT channel or in person
Give a slightly different password to be safe
Ask them to email you instead

questions.explanation: Legitimate IT support never needs your actual password. This is a classic pretexting/vishing attack — always verify identity through an independent, official channel before sharing any credentials.

questions.prompt: Why is multi-factor authentication (MFA) recommended even if you already have a strong password?

options.text: It's not necessary if the password is strong enough
It protects your account even if the password is stolen through a breach or phishing
It makes your password easier to remember
It's only useful for banking apps

questions.explanation: Passwords can be stolen through data breaches or phishing regardless of strength. MFA adds a second layer, so a stolen password alone isn't enough for an attacker to get in.

questions.prompt: You get a text message saying you have a package delivery fee to pay via a link. You weren't expecting a delivery. What is this most likely an example of?

options.text: Vishing
Smishing
A legitimate courier notification
Ransomware

questions.explanation: This is smishing (SMS phishing) — a common scam using fake delivery notifications to trick users into clicking malicious links or entering payment details.

questions.prompt: What's the best defense against ransomware locking your files?

options.text: Paying the ransom immediately if it happens
Keeping regular offline/offsite backups of important data
Using a very long password on your computer
Disabling your firewall

questions.explanation: Regular offline backups (following the 3-2-1 rule) mean you can restore your files without paying attackers, since ransomware primarily threatens data availability.

questions.prompt: Which URL is most likely to be a phishing attempt impersonating a bank called 'SecureBank'?

options.text: https://www.securebank.com/login
https://securebank.com.verify-account-now.net/login
https://online.securebank.com/login
https://www.securebank.com/help

questions.explanation: The real domain here is 'verify-account-now.net' — 'securebank.com' is just a misleading subdomain prefix designed to look legitimate at a glance.
